summary: This memo explains how Internet registration services, such as assigning names and numbers, were moving from the DDN NIC to the new InterNIC after a National Science Foundation award. It is informational and describes a transition of responsibility.

plainLanguage.summary: The office that hands out Internet names and numbers was changing hands. This paper tells people who would be doing the job next.

subtitle: Moving Internet registration services to a new organization

tldr.problem: The Defense Data Network (DDN) NIC was responsible for Internet registration, but the National Science Foundation wanted to move this service to a new organization called the InterNIC.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC announces a transition period where both organizations handle registration requests, then describes how the InterNIC will take over with new procedures and automated processing.
tldr.outcome: Non-DDN network registrations moved to the InterNIC by April 1993, with contact information and new registration templates provided for users.

today: The InterNIC registration services operated for several decades before being restructured again. Today, domain registration and IP address allocation are handled by regional Internet registries and ICANN-accredited registrars, but the InterNIC era marked the first major professionalization of Internet registration services.

sections.title: The Registration Service Transition
sections.content: This memo announces the transition of Internet registration services from the DDN Network Information Center (NIC) to a new organization called the InterNIC, which was created following a National Science Foundation award. Registration services assign domain names, IP addresses, and Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) to Internet users. The transition was necessary to handle the growing Internet and to separate military (DDN) registrations from non-military Internet registrations.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who give out internet names and numbers were changing jobs. DDN (the military part) would stay in one office, and everyone else would go to a new office called InterNIC.

sections.title: How the Transition Worked
sections.content: The transition occurred in two phases. From March 1 through March 31, 1993, both the old DDN NIC and the new InterNIC accepted registration requests using the old templates. DDN users continued to contact hostmast@nic.ddn.mil or registrar@nic.ddn.mil. Non-DDN users could send requests to either location. Starting April 1, 1993, the InterNIC took over all non-DDN registrations, requiring new templates and new email addresses. The old DDN NIC retained only DDN registrations and continued to serve military users.
sections.plainLanguage: For one month both offices took requests. After that, the InterNIC took over for non-military registrations, and the DDN office only handled military networks.

sections.title: The New Automated Registration System
sections.content: The InterNIC introduced an automated registration system called autoreg that was more efficient than the previous manual process. Users submitted a completed template to autoreg@internic.net. The system automatically parsed the template, checked for conflicts (such as duplicate domain names), and sent a verification email back to the requestor. The requestor reviewed the parsed data, corrected any errors if needed, and returned the verification form to verify@internic.net. If the verification succeeded, the registration staff completed the final processing. Requests that were not verified within seven days expired and had to be resubmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of having a person read every form by hand, the new system was automated. A computer checked the forms for mistakes and sent back confirmation. People fixed any problems and the computer confirmed again.

sections.title: Services and Contact Information
sections.content: Both registration sites provided WHOIS services to look up existing registrations. Users could check registration request status in two ways: by using the finger utility with a trouble ticket number, or by connecting to rs.internic.net via telnet and running the status command. The InterNIC provided additional services over telnet including Gopher and WAIS search tools. Root zone files (the DNS root database) were available from both sites initially, but after the transition only the InterNIC maintained them. The InterNIC also provided a mailing list (rs-info@internic.net) for announcements about registration issues and procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: People could look up who owned a domain, check if their registration was finished, and get news about changes. The InterNIC gave out a phone number too: 1-800-444-4345.
